title: eBPF‑Secure: A Lightweight eBPF‑Based Confinement and Observability Framework for Container Security
authors: Shiva Kumar Bommakanti
venue: International Journal of Intelligent Systems and Data Science
abstract: As container adoption accelerates, the need for runtime security and transparent observability has never been greater. Traditional Linux confinement primitives, namespaces, cgroups, seccomp, and LSMs are powerful but often complex to combine and difficult to extend. In this work, we introduce extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) ‑ Secure, a unified eBPF‑based framework that dynamically injects security and observability logic into the kernel without requiring recompilation or reboot. By attaching eBPF programs to key syscall and LSM hooks, eBPF‑Secure enforces container-specific policies for filesystem, network, and IPC interactions, while simultaneously gathering rich audit data into kernel‑space maps for real‑time monitoring. Two prototypes, an application sandbox and its container‑focused successor, demonstrate that eBPF‑Secure can model least‑privilege confinement, bridge the semantic gap between policy and enforcement, and deliver precise security controls with only modest performance overhead. Our evaluation against established benchmarks and an informal attack analysis shows eBPF‑Secure’s ability to harden container deployments while providing operators with fine‑grained visibility into runtime behavior, paving the way for more secure, observable, and extensible container platforms.

title: Down the pipe: A SoK on eBPF pipeline security
authors: Cinthya Celina Tamayo Gonzalez; Gabriele Costa; Simone Soderi
abstract: The extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) has emerged as a powerful mechanism for extending kernel functionality. It enables observability, security monitoring, and network control. The reliability of this system depends on a pipeline encompassing compilation, static verification, and in-kernel execution. Each of these stages depends on some safety constraints and operational assumptions. We start by explaining this pipeline from a security standpoint, with an emphasis on the coherence of its elements’ security assumptions. Building on this, we present a review of the existing methods for identifying security flaws and the proposed techniques in the literature for strengthening the eBPF ecosystem. Our review indicates that fuzz testing is the most prevalent and effective approach for identifying both bugs and vulnerabiliies. Furthermore, modifications of prior attacks offer targeted insights into high-impact weaknesses. A comparison with publicly disclosed Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) reveals a significant misalignment between academic focus and real-world failure patterns. Specifically, maps and helpers subsystems account for some of the most present vulnerabilities but receive limited attention in published research. Additionally, we have categorized the existing defensive proposals, with notable trends identified in memory isolation, verifier redesign, and runtime hardening. These findings underscore structural gaps in the current literature and motivate the development of more integrated approaches.

title: eBPF Security in the Wild: Structural Concentration, Failure Mechanisms, and Discovery Gaps
authors: Baihong Chen; Hua Ming; Weifeng Pan; Tian Xie; Xiaojun Qi; Wen Li
abstract: <div>  Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) is a security-critical in-kernel execution framework, yet its vulnerability landscape remains fragmented across components, semantic gaps, and testing techniques. We present an empirical study of observed eBPF vulnerabilities. We construct a multi-source dataset from Linux kernel fixing commits, syzbot reports, and public CVE/NVD records, and analyze it through a unified framework covering structural concentration, mechanism-level failure modes, architectural distribution, and discovery gaps in representative techniques.&nbsp; </div> <div>  <br> </div> <div>  Our results show that the observed eBPF vulnerability landscape is structurally concentrated rather than broadly dispersed across many unrelated weakness types. The dominant portion is associated with a limited set of recurring system-level failures, especially in runtime execution, concurrency, object lifecycle management, and semantic inconsistencies across trusted stages. These failures are unevenly distributed across the eBPF pipeline: Runtime is the dominant exposure surface, whereas the Verifier and JIT are lowerfrequency but structurally distinct security boundaries. A rubric-based comparison of representative techniques and a version-aligned Syzkaller case study on Linux v5.10 show that, despite visible raw coverage of Runtime, Verifier, and JIT, effective exploration is semantically narrow, and observed discoveries concentrate in a small subset of Runtime failures. Overall, raw coverage alone provides an incomplete view of discovery effectiveness. </div>
